paragraphs: Imitation learning teaches an agent to act from demonstrations. Generative adversarial imitation learning, or GAIL, does this by matching how frequently an expert visits different combinations of states and actions. The agent repeatedly updates its policy to make its own behavior resemble that pattern. Even when relatively few expert demonstrations suffice, collecting new agent trajectories during training can remain expensive.

The paper introduces a Bayesian version of GAIL in which both the policy and the cost function are stochastic neural networks. This formulation represents these components probabilistically. In particular, the cost has a predictive distribution that provides information beyond a single predicted value, and the proposed approach uses that distribution to improve learning efficiency.

Across an extensive collection of imitation tasks with high-dimensional states and actions, the authors report significantly better sample efficiency. The contribution therefore addresses the cost of gathering experience during imitation, rather than only the scarcity of demonstrations. Its stated result is that probabilistic cost predictions can make the adversarial imitation process more economical in its use of samples.
neurips-2018-a-bayesian-approach-to-gene.tldr: A Bayesian formulation of adversarial imitation learning uses probabilistic cost predictions to improve sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection asks whether a point falls in a region where the data distribution has little probability density. Calibrated anomaly detection adds another requirement: the system should also produce a confidence score for calling that point unusual. The paper develops a learning objective that connects these two outputs, so detection and confidence estimation can be addressed within one framework.

Starting from a classification approach to anomaly detection, the authors modify a proper loss function. Minimizing the resulting loss produces density estimates specifically for anomalous instances. This targeted estimation is central to the approach: the objective supplies density information in the part of the distribution relevant to identifying anomalies.

The framework also supports quantile control through a connection to a generalized pinball loss. For scoring functions built with kernels, the authors derive an efficient optimization approach using a result from point process theory. A close relative of the one-class support vector machine appears as a special case, connecting the proposed calibrated objective to an established anomaly-detection formulation.
neurips-2018-a-loss-framework-for-calibr.tldr: A modified classification loss combines anomaly detection with confidence estimation, quantile control, and efficient kernel-based optimization.

paragraphs: Isotonic regression fits values subject to an ordering constraint. This paper extends the problem to objectives that separate across individual values but can be nonconvex, with particular attention to estimators used in robust regression. Nonconvexity makes finding a globally good solution more demanding, so the authors study algorithms with explicit guarantees on how close their answer is to the global minimum.

A straightforward dynamic programming method reaches a requested accuracy ε in time that grows linearly with both the dimension and 1/ε. The proposed alternative combines techniques from convex isotonic regression with branch-and-bound ideas. Its pruning strategy takes advantage of the objective's shape, allowing the computation to adapt to structure in the particular optimization problem.

The authors report that the algorithm matches the best bounds for the general nonconvex and convex cases, with logarithmic dependence on 1/ε in the convex case. It also runs substantially faster in practice than straightforward dynamic programming, especially when high accuracy is requested. The result combines global-accuracy guarantees with practical savings from exploiting objective structure.
neurips-2018-an-efficient-pruning-algori.tldr: A pruning algorithm exploits objective structure to solve robust isotonic regression efficiently while preserving global-accuracy guarantees.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein generative adversarial network compares distributions of images using a distance that ultimately depends on how individual images are compared. That underlying choice matters: it determines which image differences contribute to the training objective. The paper starts from the observation that prior WGAN work had used the ordinary ℓ² distance for this purpose.

The authors extend the theory of WGANs with gradient penalties to Banach spaces. This broader mathematical setting allows different norms to define image distance, giving practitioners a way to choose which features the generator should emphasize. The paper examines several such choices, with particular attention to Sobolev norms and their effect on the model.

Experiments on CIFAR-10 and CelebA show improved performance for an appropriate choice of norm. The finding supports treating the underlying image distance as a meaningful modeling decision. It does not establish that every alternative norm improves generation; the reported benefit depends on choosing one that works well for the task. The contribution combines that empirical result with a theoretical framework for making such choices.
neurips-2018-banach-wasserstein-gan-3172.tldr: Extending gradient-penalty WGANs to Banach spaces lets image-distance choices emphasize different features and can improve generation.

paragraphs: Vision-language systems need to select relevant visual information while processing language. Learning attention for every pair of inputs across the two modalities can be computationally expensive. Separate attention distributions reduce that burden, but the paper argues that they neglect interactions between the modalities. Bilinear Attention Networks, or BAN, are designed to represent those interactions more directly.

BAN learns bilinear attention across two groups of input channels. Low-rank bilinear pooling builds a joint representation for each pair, providing a way to capture cross-modal relationships while addressing the cost of pairwise modeling. The authors also introduce a variant of a multimodal residual network that efficiently uses eight attention maps from BAN.

The model is evaluated both quantitatively and qualitatively on VQA 2.0 and Flickr30k Entities. The authors report significant improvements over previous methods and state-of-the-art results on both datasets. These findings support the value of attention that explicitly models relationships between visual and language inputs, together with an architecture that can efficiently combine multiple attention maps.
neurips-2018-bilinear-attention-networks.tldr: Bilinear Attention Networks efficiently model vision-language interactions and report state-of-the-art results on two multimodal benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper treats a neural network's depth and connections as structures that can be learned from dependencies in the input distribution. Its unsupervised approach represents conditional independencies hierarchically, so the resulting structure inherently determines network depth. The aim is to give architectural choices a statistical foundation through relationships present in the data.

The method reformulates neural architecture construction as Bayesian network structure learning. It first learns a generative graph, builds a stochastic inverse of that graph, and then constructs a discriminative graph for prediction. The authors prove that conditional-dependency relationships among latent variables in the generative graph are preserved in the class-conditional discriminative graph.

On image classification benchmarks, the learned structures replace the deepest convolutional and dense layers of common networks with substantially smaller alternatives while maintaining classification accuracy, reported as state of the art on the tested benchmarks. Structure learning also has a small computational cost and runs efficiently on a standard desktop CPU. The results link a principled graph-construction procedure to compact predictive networks without a costly architecture-learning process.
neurips-2018-constructing-deep-neural-ne.tldr: Learning Bayesian network structure provides a principled way to construct smaller deep-network layers while preserving tested classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks can improve accuracy by becoming deeper and wider, but their resource demands make deployment difficult in settings such as mobile applications. This paper examines the convolution operation itself as a place to reduce those demands. The authors show that a standard convolution can be decomposed into a spatial shift operation and a pointwise convolution.

To make that decomposition adaptable, they introduce the active shift layer. Its shift amounts are expressed through learnable parameters, allowing the network to adjust the movement of features during training. These parameters can be optimized through backpropagation as part of the full network, and the authors describe the layer as capable of providing optimal shift values.

The layer is incorporated into a lightweight, fast network that the authors report surpasses existing state-of-the-art networks. The significance is the connection between an operational decomposition and a trainable architecture: spatial shifting becomes something the model can learn alongside its other parameters. This gives the proposed efficient network a mechanism for adapting its convolution-like processing to the task.
neurips-2018-constructing-fast-network-t.tldr: A learnable spatial-shift layer helps turn decomposed convolutions into a lightweight network with strong reported performance.

paragraphs: When many agents share a system-wide reward, it can be difficult to determine which decisions helped the group. This paper studies a class of multiagent problems where agents affect one another through their collective influence rather than their identities. The setting is relevant to urban systems and includes uncertainty and partial observability.

The authors allow the reward to be nondecomposable, meaning it cannot simply be split into separate rewards for individual agents. They develop collective actor-critic reinforcement learning methods that address credit assignment and produce low-variance policy-gradient estimates. They also develop credit-assignment methods based on difference rewards for this collective setting.

The goal of these estimates is faster convergence to high-quality solutions despite having only a global reward. Empirical evaluations cover taxi fleet optimization, multiagent patrolling, and a synthetic grid-navigation problem. The proposed approaches produce significantly better solutions than previous methods in those evaluations. The findings show how exploiting collective interaction structure can help learning systems use shared feedback even when individual contributions are not supplied directly.
neurips-2018-credit-assignment-for-colle.tldr: Collective actor-critic and difference-reward methods improve multiagent credit assignment when agents share a nondecomposable global reward.

paragraphs: Online portfolio management chooses investments repeatedly as new market outcomes arrive. This paper studies the tradeoff between a regret guarantee and the computation needed to obtain it. Cover's Universal Portfolio achieves optimal regret of order N ln T for N financial instruments over T rounds, but its implementation requires log-concave sampling and has a large polynomial running time.

The proposed algorithm uses Online Mirror Descent with a new regularizer. It is presented as the first algorithm with a logarithmic regret guarantee that does not build on Universal Portfolio. Its bound is of order N²(ln T)⁴, larger than Universal Portfolio's bound but still depending on time through powers of a logarithm.

Standard optimization methods can implement the algorithm in order TN^2.5 time per round. The contribution is therefore a different balance between theoretical performance and implementation cost. The authors contrast it with other existing approaches whose regret either grows polynomially with T or includes a potentially unbounded factor, such as the inverse of the smallest price relative.
neurips-2018-efficient-online-portfolio-.tldr: A new mirror-descent portfolio algorithm trades a larger logarithmic regret bound for a faster implementation than Universal Portfolio.

paragraphs: Hierarchical generative models describe observations through layers of hidden variables. Learning with these models requires inference about which hidden-variable configurations could explain an observation. This paper introduces the distributed distributional code Helmholtz machine, emphasizing the flexibility and accuracy of that inference process as a central part of model learning.

The approach learns an explicit recognition model that approximates the posterior distribution over hidden variables. It shares this broad strategy with Helmholtz machines and variational autoencoders, but changes how the posterior is represented. The representation is neither restricted to a narrow, tractable parameterized family nor expressed as a collection of samples.

An extended wake-sleep algorithm trains both the generative and recognition models. This enables learning hierarchical models containing discrete as well as continuous variables, where accurate posterior representations are important. Experiments on synthetic data, natural image patches, and MNIST show the algorithm outperforming the state-of-the-art methods considered. The contribution ties a more flexible representation of uncertainty to a training procedure capable of using it.
neurips-2018-flexible-and-accurate-infer.tldr: A new Helmholtz-machine approach pairs flexible posterior representations with extended wake-sleep training for hierarchical generative models.

paragraphs: Training a latent-variable model often requires gradients involving continuous random variables. The reparameterization trick is useful because it provides an efficient way to compute gradients with low variance. However, the classic form does not apply to several important distributions, restricting where that training technique can be used.

The paper introduces an alternative way to compute reparameterization gradients through implicit differentiation. This changes the mathematical route used to obtain the gradients and broadens the range of supported distributions. The authors demonstrate the approach on Gamma, Beta, Dirichlet, and von Mises distributions, which they identify as incompatible with the classic reparameterization trick.

Experiments show the proposed method to be faster and more accurate than existing gradient estimators for those distributions. The result matters because the choice of random-variable distribution is part of how a latent-variable model is specified. Extending efficient gradient computation to additional distributions makes the training approach applicable to a broader set of such models, with the reported speed and accuracy benefits established by the experiments.
neurips-2018-implicit-reparameterization.tldr: Implicit differentiation extends reparameterization gradients to additional continuous distributions, with faster and more accurate estimation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A highly accurate deep network may be unsuitable when a deployed model must be interpretable or fit into a severely constrained memory budget. ProfWeight transfers information from such a pretrained network to a simpler model or a very shallow network. Its motivation includes both understandable predictions and deployment on devices such as sensors.

The method examines intermediate representations inside the deep network. Linear probes applied to flattened representations produce confidence scores at different layers. ProfWeight uses these scores to assign weights to training examples for the simpler model, through a weighting procedure the authors support theoretically. Information from the deep model thus influences which examples receive emphasis during training.

On CIFAR-10, the authors report improvements of 3–4% for networks containing only a fraction of the ResNet blocks in the complex model. On a manufacturing problem, they report roughly a 13% increase in the test accuracy of a CART model, the domain standard. These results show that intermediate-layer confidence can be useful for improving models whose simplicity is important to their intended deployment.
neurips-2018-improving-simple-models-wit.tldr: ProfWeight uses confidence from a deep network's intermediate layers to weight training examples and improve simpler models.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation uses a teacher model to help train a smaller model with good generalization. A strong pretrained teacher can provide useful guidance, but preparing it creates a separate training phase. Existing online approaches avoid that two-stage procedure, while the paper identifies their lack of a high-capacity teacher as a drawback.

On-the-fly Native Ensemble, or ONE, builds a strong teacher during the same training process as the target network. It trains a single network with multiple branches and establishes the teacher on the fly. This provides a one-stage online distillation strategy in which teacher construction and target-model learning happen together.

Evaluations cover a variety of deep networks on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, SVHN, and ImageNet. The authors report larger generalization improvements than alternative methods, together with computational-efficiency advantages. The contribution is a way to combine the guidance of a strong teacher with a unified training procedure. Its reported benefits concern both the quality of the learned models and the efficiency of obtaining them.
neurips-2018-knowledge-distillation-by-o.tldr: ONE creates a strong teacher inside a single multi-branch training process, improving online knowledge distillation and reported generalization.

paragraphs: Beam search is a common way to approximately decode structured predictions by maintaining several candidate solutions during search. Many models use this procedure when making predictions but are trained without explicitly accounting for it. The paper focuses on that mismatch: a model that will rely on a beam should also learn how to use it.

The authors develop a general framework for learning beam-search policies through imitation learning. Within this formulation, the beam is part of the model itself. Training therefore addresses behavior within the search procedure, making the way candidates are handled a component of what is learned.

The resulting meta-algorithm encompasses existing learning algorithms and suggests additional ones. It also supports new no-regret guarantees for learning beam-search policies. These are theoretical contributions about learning within the framework, rather than claims that approximate decoding always finds the best structured output. The paper's significance is to unify beam-aware training approaches and provide a basis for designing and analyzing further policies.
neurips-2018-learning-beam-search-polici.tldr: An imitation-learning framework makes beam search part of the learned model and provides new no-regret guarantees.

paragraphs: In repeated auctions, a bidder may sacrifice an immediate benefit to influence what happens in later rounds. This creates a challenge for learning a reserve price: even if each individual auction encourages truthful bidding, bidders who care about the future may act strategically across auctions. The paper studies reserve-price learning under that behavior.

The authors introduce algorithms with small regret under either of two conditions. One is a large market, defined so that no bidder appears in a constant fraction of the rounds. The other is bidder impatience, expressed by discounting future utility by a factor mildly bounded away from one. These are alternative conditions supporting the guarantees.

The approach carefully manages the information revealed to each bidder. It draws on differentially private online learning and jointly differentially private algorithms. This information control is the central mechanism for handling strategic participation. The result establishes that useful learning guarantees remain possible in the stated settings, where previous approaches such as empirical pricing do not generally provide nontrivial regret guarantees.
neurips-2018-learning-optimal-reserve-pr.tldr: Information-controlled auction algorithms achieve small regret against forward-looking bidders when markets are large or bidders are sufficiently impatient.

paragraphs: Deep learning for electronic health records can demand more training data than a healthcare system has available. External medical ontologies may help, but terminology inconsistencies can make them difficult or unhelpful to use. MiME addresses data insufficiency by drawing on relationships already encoded within the health records themselves.

The method learns representations of the records' multilevel structure, including relationships among medical codes. Alongside this representation learning, it performs auxiliary prediction tasks derived from that structure. These tasks do not require external labels, allowing the model to use the organization of existing records as an additional source of training information.

The authors evaluate heart-failure prediction and sequential disease prediction, reporting improvements over baselines across diverse settings. For heart-failure prediction, MiME consistently beats all baselines across different dataset sizes. Its largest improvement occurs on the smallest dataset: a 15% relative gain in precision-recall area under the curve over the strongest baseline. This finding supports the usefulness of modeling internal record structure when available training data are especially limited.
neurips-2018-mime-multilevel-medical-emb.tldr: MiME uses the internal hierarchy of health records and auxiliary prediction tasks to improve healthcare prediction, especially with limited data.

paragraphs: Missing observations make multivariate time series harder to analyze. Filling gaps with means or zeros, deleting incomplete cases, and using matrix factorization do not capture the temporal dependencies and complex distributions emphasized in this paper. The authors instead formulate imputation as a generation problem: learn the data distribution and use it to produce missing values.

Their method trains a generative adversarial network on a multivariate time-series dataset. Because recorded sequences are themselves incomplete and temporally irregular, the network includes a modified gated recurrent unit to model that irregularity. This adapts the generative approach to the structure of time-series data rather than treating the observations like complete images.

Experiments on two datasets show more accurate imputation than the evaluated baselines. The authors also find that a simple prediction model applied to the completed data can achieve state-of-the-art results on the prediction tasks. This connects the quality of generated replacements to downstream usefulness: better imputation can help subsequent analysis, beyond improving the missing-value estimates considered on their own.
neurips-2018-multivariate-time-series-im.tldr: A GAN adapted to incomplete, irregular time series generates missing values and improves both imputation and downstream prediction in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Neural Architecture Optimization, or NAO, searches for network designs through continuous optimization. The paper targets the inefficiency of searching directly over discrete architectures with reinforcement learning or evolutionary methods. Its central idea is to represent architectures in a space where gradients can suggest promising changes.

Three components support this process. An encoder maps an architecture to a continuous representation, a predictor estimates accuracy from that representation, and a decoder converts it back into a network design. Gradients through the predictor guide the search toward an embedding with potentially better accuracy. The decoder then turns that candidate into an architecture.

The authors report competitive results with substantially reduced computation: 2.11% test error on CIFAR-10 and 56.0 test perplexity on PTB. The best designs also transfer successfully to CIFAR-100 and WikiText-2. With weight sharing, the method reports 3.53% CIFAR-10 error and 56.6 PTB perplexity while using less than 10 GPU hours for both tasks. These findings support continuous representations as a useful route to efficient architecture search.
neurips-2018-neural-architecture-optimiz.tldr: NAO encodes network architectures into a continuous space, improves their predicted accuracy with gradients, and decodes promising new designs.

paragraphs: Persistent homology summarizes topological structure using persistence diagrams, which are multisets of points rather than ordinary feature vectors. Kernel methods offer a way to use these diagrams in machine learning, but the geometry used to compare them matters. The paper identifies an obstacle with Wasserstein distance: it lacks negative definiteness, limiting direct construction of positive definite kernels without approximation.

The authors instead use Fisher information geometry to construct the Persistence Fisher kernel. Its positive definiteness does not depend on approximation. They analyze the eigensystem of the kernel's induced integral operator and use that analysis to derive generalization-error bounds through covering numbers and Rademacher averages.

The paper also establishes stability and infinite divisibility, and supplies a separate approximation whose cost is linear in the number of diagram points and whose error is bounded. Experiments across several tasks and benchmark datasets compare favorably with other persistence-diagram kernels. The contribution combines a geometrically motivated exact kernel, theoretical guarantees, and a faster approximation for practical computation.
neurips-2018-persistence-fisher-kernel-a.tldr: The Persistence Fisher kernel uses Fisher geometry to compare persistence diagrams with positive definiteness, theoretical guarantees, and a bounded-error fast approximation.

paragraphs: Training a neural network across CPUs and GPUs requires deciding where each operation should run. Those placement decisions affect total training time. Existing reinforcement-learning approaches learn placements through repeated Monte Carlo experiments, and this paper argues that treating placement samples equally leaves room to improve the search.

Post combines cross-entropy minimization with proximal policy optimization. It represents placements using discrete probability distributions, making the cross-entropy method usable as a sampling technique. Maximum likelihood estimation then estimates an optimal probability mass. The authors present the joint algorithm as achieving a theoretical guarantee of optimal efficiency.

The system is implemented on Google Cloud and evaluated using several popular neural-network training benchmarks. Given the same amount of time to learn placements, Post finds placements that reduce training time by as much as 63.7% relative to the state of the art. That figure is the largest reported reduction, rather than a uniform improvement across all cases. The practical result links better placement search to faster execution of the training workload.
neurips-2018-post-device-placement-with-.tldr: Post combines probabilistic sampling and policy optimization to find device placements with up to 63.7% shorter training times in reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: SplineNets make convolutional-network computation depend on both the input and the computational path already taken. They generalize neural decision graphs continuously, allowing an individual sample to activate only a subset of nodes. The goal is to reduce computation while maintaining or potentially improving accuracy.

Instead of selecting a branch from a categorical distribution, a sample selects a continuous position that identifies function weights, such as convolution filters. Compact B-splines parameterize smooth, low-dimensional manifolds containing infinitely many possible weights. A unified loss controls smoothness across network and decision parameters, connecting flexible function selection with structured learning.

The authors also use mutual information between spline positions and class labels to encourage effective utilization and specialization for classification. Experiments show significant ResNet accuracy gains with negligible speed cost. In the reported comparison, a 32-level SplineNet matches the precision of a 110-level ResNet. This demonstrates that input-dependent, continuous selection of functions can make a shallower network competitive with a substantially deeper one in the tested setting.
neurips-2018-splinenets-continuous-neura.tldr: SplineNets select input-dependent functions from smooth weight manifolds, improving reported accuracy while keeping computation economical.

paragraphs: Importance sampling can accelerate supervised learning by giving some training examples higher sampling priority. The theoretical benefit comes with a practical expense: determining those priorities can itself require substantial computation. This paper focuses on that overhead, which can prevent a better sampling strategy from delivering a useful reduction in total training time.

The proposed procedure, robust approximate importance sampling, or RAIS, approximates the ideal sampling distribution using robust optimization. It is designed for stochastic gradient descent. The objective is to retain much of exact importance sampling's benefit while greatly reducing the work required to decide which examples to sample.

Empirically, RAIS-SGD and standard SGD trace similar learning curves, but RAIS progresses through them more quickly. The authors report speedups of at least 20% in their experiments, with larger gains in some cases. The result highlights an implementation-sensitive aspect of learning algorithms: a theoretically advantageous sampling rule becomes useful when its own computational cost is sufficiently small. Here, approximation is the mechanism that makes that tradeoff favorable.
neurips-2018-training-deep-models-faster.tldr: RAIS approximates importance sampling cheaply enough to accelerate SGD, with reported experimental speedups of at least 20%.

paragraphs: Image captioning converts an image into text, while text-to-image generation works in the opposite direction. This paper treats the two tasks as complementary sources of training feedback. Its turbo-learning approach jointly trains an image-to-text generator, called CaptionBot, and a text-to-image generator, called DrawingBot.

The generators form a closed loop: an input passes through one model and then the other, returning to its original type. The authors introduce an additional loss that compares the original input with the result of that round trip. This feedback supplements the losses already used to train each generator and connects their learning processes.

The same loop can generate pseudo-labels for unlabeled examples, enabling semi-supervised learning. On COCO, the authors report large, significant performance improvements for both generators compared with training them separately. The contribution is therefore useful in two related ways: the paired tasks provide an additional learning signal for one another, and their outputs make otherwise unlabeled samples usable within the joint training approach.
neurips-2018-turbo-learning-for-captionb.tldr: Turbo learning jointly trains captioning and image-generation models through closed-loop feedback, improving both and enabling semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Motion-Oriented Reinforcement Learning, or MOREL, gives an agent a representation of moving objects before it learns how to act from visual observations. The method detects and segments objects without supervision by using motion structure and flow information in video. Those object representations then guide the policy's attention during action selection.

As learning proceeds, the agent identifies which moving objects matter for decisions and gradually builds a policy around them. This separates the discovery of useful visual structure from the task of choosing actions. The approach makes moving objects an explicit part of the information the policy uses.

Experiments on a suite of Atari games show that detecting moving objects reduces the environmental interaction needed to obtain a good policy. The resulting policies are also more interpretable than direct black-box mappings from images to actions or values. Inspecting each detected object's segmentation and motion gives practitioners a way to examine whether the policy relies on sensible information. The reported benefits therefore include both learning efficiency and visibility into the policy's visual basis.
neurips-2018-unsupervised-video-object-s.tldr: MOREL learns moving-object representations from video to reduce reinforcement-learning interaction needs and make visual policies easier to inspect.

paragraphs: Visual Object Networks, or VONs, generate object images through an explicit three-dimensional representation. The paper addresses the gap between producing realistic two-dimensional images and representing the underlying 3D world. Inspired by graphics rendering, it separates image formation into shape, viewpoint, and texture, modeled as conditionally independent factors.

The generation process first synthesizes a 3D shape, then renders its silhouette and depth map from a sampled viewpoint. These intermediate outputs are called 2.5D sketches. A final stage adds realistic texture to produce an image. An end-to-end adversarial framework jointly learns the 3D shape and 2D texture components.

The authors report more realistic images than state-of-the-art 2D synthesis methods. The separated representation also enables viewpoint changes, shape and texture editing, interpolation through shape and texture spaces, and appearance transfer across objects and viewpoints. These capabilities connect image generation to controllable 3D operations: the model exposes factors that can be changed individually instead of leaving the entire image-formation process implicit in a single representation.
neurips-2018-visual-object-networks-imag.tldr: VON generates images through separated shape, viewpoint, and texture factors, enabling realistic synthesis and controllable 3D editing.
